title: THE HIDDEN WEB
subtitle: The data of the internet travels through cables lying on the seabed — a network laid over 170 years, still at the mercy of nets, anchors, whales, and the rivalries of nations.

beats.text: The data of the internet travels through cables lying on the seabed — a network laid over 170 years, still at the mercy of nets, anchors, whales, and the rivalries of nations.
beats.label: THE QUESTION

beats.text: The answer sits inside a chain of specialized decisions and infrastructure.
beats.label: THE SYSTEM

beats.text: Submarine cables carry 99 percent of the data traffic that crosses the world's oceans.
beats.label: ARTICLE

beats.text: A submarine cable moves data in the terabits per second, while a satellite typically offers about one gigabit per second: a ratio of more than 1000 to 1.
beats.label: ARTICLE

beats.text: Satellites handle less than five percent of global data transmission, a share some estimates put as low as 0.5 percent.
beats.label: ARTICLE

beats.text: Modern undersea cables are typically about 25 millimetres in diameter and weigh around 1.4 tonnes per kilometre in their deep-sea sections.
beats.label: ARTICLE

beats.text: Most cable routes run through deep water, where the seabed grants a measure of protection from fishing and storms.
beats.label: ARTICLE

beats.text: Antarctica is the only continent still without a submarine cable link, so its bases rely on satellite relays with limited capacity.
beats.label: ARTICLE

beats.text: An Antarctic fiber cable would have to survive minus 80 degrees Celsius and ice sheets moving up to 10 metres every year.
beats.label: ARTICLE

beats.text: Melting Arctic ice has opened routes for projects like Polar Express, spanning 12,650 kilometres, and Far North Fiber, spanning 14,500.
beats.label: ARTICLE

beats.text: The internet relies on a web of cables whose exact positions are public knowledge.
beats.label: ARTICLE

beats.text: The First Threads
beats.label: PART 2

beats.text: In 1842 Samuel Morse submerged a wire insulated with tarred hemp and India rubber in New York Harbor and telegraphed through it.
beats.label: ARTICLE

beats.text: Early telegraph cables wrapped a copper core in gutta-percha, a natural polymer with almost ideal insulating properties.
beats.label: ARTICLE

beats.text: The first transatlantic telegraph cable became operational on 16 August 1858, linking two continents for the first time in an instant.
beats.label: ARTICLE

beats.text: That first 1858 cable worked for only about a month before the technology of the day failed it.
beats.label: ARTICLE

beats.text: Attempts in 1865 and 1866 aboard the world's largest steamship, the SS Great Eastern, produced the first successful transatlantic cable.
beats.label: ARTICLE

beats.text: British companies owned two-thirds of the world's cables in 1892, and by 1923 their share was still 42.7 percent.
beats.label: ARTICLE
sources: Wikipedia · British dominance of early cable

beats.text: By 1872 every continent except Antarctica had been linked by submarine telecommunications cables.
beats.label: ARTICLE

beats.text: In 1896 the world had 30 cable-laying ships, and 24 of them were British.
beats.label: ARTICLE
sources: Wikipedia · British dominance of early cable

beats.text: Britain's first act after declaring war on Germany in 1914 was to cut the five cables linking Germany with France, Spain and the Azores.
beats.label: ARTICLE
sources: Wikipedia · British dominance of early cable

beats.text: The first trans-Pacific telegraph cables were completed in 1902 and 1903, linking the United States to Hawaii, Guam and the Philippines.
beats.label: ARTICLE
sources: Wikipedia · Submarine cables across the Pacific, 1902-1991

beats.text: The Voice Cables
beats.label: PART 3

beats.text: TAT-1, the first transatlantic telephone cable, was inaugurated on 25 September 1956 carrying 36 telephone channels.
beats.label: ARTICLE

beats.text: Early telephone repeaters were powered by high-voltage direct current sent down the cable's inner conductor.
beats.label: ARTICLE

beats.text: TAT-8, the first fiber-optic transatlantic cable, went into operation in 1988 with two working fiber pairs and one backup.
beats.label: ARTICLE

beats.text: The first-generation cable repeaters remain among the most reliable vacuum tube amplifiers ever designed.
beats.label: ARTICLE

beats.text: Many 1960s coaxial cables are still usable but were abandoned because their capacity is too small to be commercially viable.
beats.label: ARTICLE

beats.text: Cable capacity grew so large that satellites could no longer back it up, forcing nets to reroute around the seabed instead.
beats.label: ARTICLE

beats.text: In 1942 submarine cable technology was adapted to create the world's first submarine oil pipeline, Operation Pluto.
beats.label: ARTICLE

beats.text: The Modern Web
beats.label: PART 4

beats.text: Modern optical repeaters use erbium-doped fiber amplifiers, first installed in submarine cables in 1995.
beats.label: ARTICLE

beats.text: Cable repeaters are powered by a constant direct current of 3,000 to 15,000 volts, feeding up to 16.5 kilowatts into the line.
beats.label: ARTICLE

beats.text: The optical fiber in undersea cables is so clear that runs of more than 100 kilometres between repeaters are possible.
beats.label: ARTICLE

beats.text: Unrepeated cables as long as 380 kilometres were in service by 2014, carrying their own pump light to remote amplifiers.
beats.label: ARTICLE

beats.text: Wavelength-division multiplexing lets one fiber carry many laser channels at once, capped by the spacing and bandwidth of amplifiers.
beats.label: ARTICLE

beats.text: Spatial-division multiplexing cables run at least 12 fiber pairs, and cables with up to 24 pairs have been deployed.
beats.label: ARTICLE

beats.text: A 2012 trial carried error-free 100 gigabit-per-second signals across 6,000 kilometres of Atlantic route, and one cable can move tens of terabits per second.
beats.label: ARTICLE

beats.text: Fastest transatlantic round-trip latency is under 60 milliseconds, close to the speed-of-light floor for an all-sea route.
beats.label: ARTICLE

beats.text: A typical multi-terabit, transoceanic cable system costs several hundred million dollars to construct.
beats.label: ARTICLE

beats.text: A speculative rush poured more than 22 billion dollars into privately financed cables between 1999 and 2001, ending in bankruptcies like Global Crossing.
beats.label: ARTICLE

beats.text: Between 1998 and 2003 roughly 70 percent of undersea fiber-optic cable was laid in the Pacific.
beats.label: ARTICLE

beats.text: In July 2009 a cable owned in part by African investors plugged East Africa into the wider internet, delayed a month by coastal piracy.
beats.label: ARTICLE

beats.text: The Fragile Seafloor
beats.label: PART 5

beats.text: Between 1959 and 1996, fewer than 9 percent of cable breaks in the Atlantic and Caribbean were caused by natural events.
beats.label: ARTICLE

beats.text: Cable faults averaged 3.7 per 1,000 kilometres each year from 1959 to 1979, dropping to 0.44 per 1,000 kilometres after 1985.
beats.label: ARTICLE

beats.text: Widespread burial of cable beginning in 1980 cut the fault rate to a fraction of its earlier level.
beats.label: ARTICLE

beats.text: Cable breaks remain routine, with more than 50 repairs a year in the Atlantic Ocean alone and serious failures in 2006, 2008, 2009 and 2011.
beats.label: ARTICLE

beats.text: Cables in waters shallower than 2,000 metres are now regularly buried against fishing nets and bottom trawling.
beats.label: ARTICLE

beats.text: Fishing vessels are the leading cause of accidental damage to submarine communication cables.
beats.label: ARTICLE

beats.text: In 1873 a whale damaged the Persian Gulf Cable between Karachi and Gwadar, tangling its tail in loops of cable and drowning.
beats.label: ARTICLE

beats.text: Whale entanglement ruptured cables 16 times between 1877 and 1955, 13 of them involving sperm whales.
beats.label: ARTICLE

beats.text: In 2013 three divers were arrested for severing the main cable linking Egypt with Europe, drastically cutting the country's internet speed.
beats.label: ARTICLE

beats.text: The New Cold War
beats.label: PART 6

beats.text: The 2022 Tonga volcanic eruption cut the island's only cable, a break declared a national crisis that took weeks to repair.
beats.label: ARTICLE

beats.text: In February 1959, 12 breaks struck five American trans-Atlantic cables; a US naval vessel detained a Soviet trawler that had shadowed each of them.
beats.label: ARTICLE

beats.text: Two Baltic Sea cable breaks in November 2024 were called a hybrid action, because no one believed the anchors were accidental.
beats.label: ARTICLE

beats.text: Russian fishing vessels were reported passing over a damaged submarine cable up to 20 times in 2022.
beats.label: ARTICLE

beats.text: After the Nord Stream sabotage, NATO increased patrols and monitoring of undersea infrastructure.
beats.label: ARTICLE

beats.text: China's Digital Silk Road funds cable projects through firms like HMN Technologies, which holds up to 10 percent of the global market.
beats.label: ARTICLE

beats.text: Chinese involvement in roughly a quarter of global submarine cables could let its networks reroute data and apply political pressure.
beats.label: ARTICLE

beats.text: Submarine cables are governed by UNCLOS articles that protect laying and repair, yet key states such as the United States and Turkey have not ratified the treaty.
beats.label: ARTICLE

beats.text: During the Cold War the US Navy and NSA tapped Soviet undersea lines in Operation Ivy Bells.
beats.label: ARTICLE

beats.text: Shore stations can now locate a cable break with spread-spectrum reflectometry, gathering a complete data set in 20 milliseconds.
beats.label: ARTICLE

beats.text: The important detail is not any single company or machine; it is the dependency between them.
beats.label: THE CONNECTION

beats.text: The data of the internet travels through cables lying on the seabed — a network laid over 170 years, still at the mercy of nets, anchors, whales, and the rivalries of nations.
beats.label: THE THESIS
